newsitem.title: USA: Brady debt slumps as U.S. investors book profits.
newsitem.headline: Brady debt slumps as U.S. investors book profits.

text.p: Emerging market debt prices slumped Wednesday as investors booked Brady bond profits positions amid stable U.S. markets, a weaker Mexican peso and turbulent Argentine political scene, analysts said.
With little substantive news to rattle markets, U.S. investors seemed keen to bank some of the magnificent 33 percent returns posted this year,

"We've had a nice run all year and people are looking to lock in some profits," said Amy Falls, director of emerging markets research at Morgan Stanley. "It doesn't seem to be based on any major change of fundamentals."
The Brady bond market still seemed attractive on a long term basis, with the spreads of emerging debt very competitive when measured against comparably rated assets, analysts said.
Brazilian C bonds gave back 5/8 to 71-1/4, while Mexico's global bond due 2026 slipped 5/8 to 99-3/8 and Venezuelan DCBs dropped 1-1/8 to 82-3/8.
"The Brady market has really outperformed the Treasury market for a long time," said one U.S. hedge fund investor. "A lot of dealers have pumped these credits up."
News of tame U.S. consumer prices, as the September CPI rose 0.3 percent, assuaged inflation fears and soothed the U.S. bond market, but emerging debt suffered through the day.
"The underlying tone remains positive but it's true that everyone is still very focused on the peso," said Olivier Lemaigre, emerging market strategist at Citicorp Securities.
The Mexican currency ended weaker but recouped some of its losses on a third consecutive day of slippage.
Mexico's central bank governor Miguel Mancera said on Wednesday's the Banco de Mexico's monetary and foreign policies do not seek to avoid a weaker peso.
And a top Mexican finance ministry official described the recent peso volatility as "normal" and should die down as the market finds a comfortable level.

Citicorp's Lemaigre said that market was looking for a gradual peso depreciation so as to avoid a sharp decline, and that the Bank of Mexico strategy of lifting interest rates to stem excessive volatility had been sound.
"You want to see a peso depreciation not for the purpose of the trade balance but to prevent an overreaction over time," he said.
Argentina's debt suffered from the ongoing political row stemming from corruption allegations against two cabinet members leveled by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo.
Argentine FRBs fell 1-1/4 to 81-1/2, while Argentine Pars gave back 1-1/8 to 57-3/8.
The country's President Carlos Menem dismissed as lies Cavallo's charges against Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan.
But in a Reuters Financial Television interview, Cavallo said that he did not believe Menem questioned his charges and stated his belief the president would stand by a commitment to fight corruption.

"I'm just a non-believer in the Argentina story ... Ecuador looks a lot better than Argentina," the hedge fund player said. "You're going to see everyone shift and think of Ecuador as the top potential on the up side."
But Ecuador underperformed Wednesday, as the country's IEBs lost 1-3/8 to 80, and PDIs gave up 1-1/8 to 54.
-- George Lerner, 212-859-1671
